intro: Sixteen cedar seedlings came from Kew in 1818 and two are still standing in front of the palace, the larger of them the thickest of its kind in Germany. The Schlosspark is thirteen hectares of English landscape garden on ground that has been garden since 1441, and it holds five big trunks, four of them over five metres round within a few hundred metres of each other. Free to walk through, twenty-five minutes from Frankfurt.
meta_description: Five big trees in Bad Homburg's Schlosspark, one of them the thickest cedar in Germany. Free, 25 minutes from Frankfurt.
question_meta: The only dated tree in Bad Homburg's Schlosspark is the cedar planted in 1822. The oak by the bridge is wider and has never been dated.
question_answer: The oldest tree in Bad Homburg with a documented date is the larger of the two cedars in front of the palace's royal wing, planted in 1822 from seed that came out of the Royal Botanic Gardens at Kew, now 6.40 metres round and called by the city the thickest and oldest of its kind in Germany. It is very probably not the oldest tree in the park. Two pedunculate oaks, 5.39 metres at the bridge and 4.94 metres by the lake, and a plane of 5.66 metres near the wingnuts, have never been dated by anyone. All of them stand in the Schlosspark, which is free to walk through.
question_context: The honest answer here is a gap. The cedar is the only tree in the park with a year on it, because somebody wrote down when it was planted. The three wider trunks have no recorded age at all, and a girth of five metres on an oak or a plane would ordinarily mean a tree considerably older than two centuries. Joining the park's own dates to them would be guesswork: a garden is recorded beside the castle from 1441, a baroque garden was laid out from 1680, and the grounds were remade as an English landscape park a century later, but no source connects any phase to a particular tree. The measurements come from a 2021 survey by the dendrologist Rainer Lippert on baumkunde.de. The cedar's figures come from the city and from baumkunde's register, which disagree about the species, the city calling it an Atlas cedar and the register a cedar of Lebanon. A reader who knows the park well points to a third big oak, the Schöne Eiche, near the gate to the old town, which we will add once we can place it.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Bad Homburg?
faq.a: The only one with a date on it is the cedar in front of the palace's royal wing, planted in 1822. Both big oaks and the plane are wider and have never been dated.

It is 6.40 metres round with a crown spreading more than 35 metres east to west, and the city calls it the thickest and oldest of its kind in Germany. It came from Kew as one of sixteen seedlings in 1818, of which two survived.
Yes. The park is open to walk through with no gate and no ticket. The palace buildings themselves are ticketed.

faq.q: How do I get there from Frankfurt?
faq.a: The S5 reaches Bad Homburg in roughly 25 minutes, and the Schlosspark is about a ten-minute walk from the station.

faq.q: Can I see them all in one walk?
faq.a: Yes. They stand within a few hundred metres of each other in a thirteen-hectare park, the cedars by the palace and the rest around the pond and the lake.

trees.name: The Cedars of the Konigsflugel
trees.species: Cedar (Cedrus libani per baumkunde.de, Cedrus atlantica per the city of Bad Homburg; disputed, see notes)

location.address: In front of the Konigsflugel, Schlosspark, Bad Homburg vor der Hohe, 61348 Hessen, Germany

trees.story:
Sixteen cedar seedlings came from Kew and two of them are still standing here. They arrived through Princess Elizabeth of Great Britain, who married Landgrave Friedrich VI Joseph in 1818, brought her own interest in botany with her and kept her English contacts. The pair went into the ground in front of the palace's royal wing in 1822 and have grown side by side ever since.

The larger one is the point. It is 6.40 metres round, 21 metres tall, and the city calls it both the thickest and the oldest of its kind in Germany. Its reach is the part that does not photograph: by 2011 the crown measured more than 35 metres from east to west, so the tree is far wider than it is high, with limbs that run out nearly horizontally and then turn up at the ends.

Two hundred years is young for a cedar. The species can pass 800, which means this one is barely a quarter through and still thickening. Sources disagree about which cedar it actually is: the city says Atlas cedar, the German tree register says cedar of Lebanon. If you know your cedars, we would like to hear which.

trees.verify_notes:
SPECIES DISPUTED and published that way rather than resolved by us. The city of Bad Homburg's own page is internally inconsistent: it is titled Libanonzeder, and its text reads 'Die machtigere der Beiden, eine Atlaszeder, ist mit ihrem Stammumfang von 6,40 Meter nicht nur die grosste ihrer Art in ganz Deutschland, sondern auch die alteste.' baumkunde.de registers it as Libanon Zeder. The page asks the reader which, per the publish-and-ask rule.
GIRTH: the city gives 6.40m, and separately 6.09m measured at about 20cm height in October 2021 (a waist measurement, not breast height). baumkunde records 6.52m on 12 August 2021. 6.40m is used as the headline as the city's own figure; the spread between the three is measuring height rather than disagreement about the tree.
HISTORY: baumkunde records the seedlings as a gift from the Duke of Cambridge in 1818 for his sister's marriage, 16 received and 2 surviving; the city credits Princess Elizabeth's own contacts with the Royal Botanic Gardens at Kew. Adolphus, Duke of Cambridge, was Elizabeth's brother, so the two accounts are compatible, but neither source states both halves, so the story says Kew and Elizabeth and does not join them to the Duke.
ALIVE: baumkunde records the tree as vital, last visited 31 October 2024.
Photo: viewed directly. Lead is the whole tree with the palace behind it, daylight, colour, photo_light.py OK (brightness 125.0, blown 0.080). Second is the view from underneath, also OK (brightness 78.5).
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by being the wider of two cedars growing together in front of the palace's royal wing, with nearly horizontal limbs spreading more than 35 metres east to west. Nothing else on that lawn comes close.

trees.name: The Dawn Redwood by the Pond

location.address: Southern end of the park, by the pond, Schlosspark, Bad Homburg vor der Hohe, 61348 Hessen, Germany

trees.story:
This species was known only from fossils until 1944. A Chinese forester found living dawn redwoods in Hubei, seed went round the world's botanic gardens from 1948, and almost every large specimen in Europe is one of that first generation. This one is about 70 years old, which for a tree on this site makes it among the youngest here and by some distance the fastest.

In seventy years it has put on 5.8 metres of girth and 28 metres of height, which is more than the cedar managed in two hundred. The base is the part worth walking to: it flares out into deep vertical folds and buttresses, gnarled in a way that reads as far older than the tree is, and the bark runs in long fibrous strips up a trunk that tapers hard.

It is a conifer that drops its needles, so it turns foxy orange in November and stands bare through winter. Come in autumn and it is the brightest thing at the south end of the park.

best_time.label: November, when the needles turn foxy orange before dropping

trees.verify_notes: Single-sourced on the measurements: baumkunde.de register entry 4258 gives 5.8m girth (8 August 2021), 28m height, age about 70 years, condition vital, last visited 7 May 2023, and describes the 'faltig-knorrigem Stammfuss'. Flagged accordingly. de.wikipedia's Schlosspark Bad Homburg article confirms the park, its size and its public character but names no individual trees. The 1944 rediscovery and the 1948 seed distribution are the species' documented history, not a claim about this specimen; the story says almost every large European specimen is of that generation and does not assert that this one is. No photograph found under an open licence.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by a trunk base that flares into deep vertical folds and buttresses, with bark in long fibrous strips, standing at the pond at the southern end of the park. In winter it is the tall bare conifer.

trees.name: The Oak at the Bridge

location.address: Left of the bridge at the northern end of the pond, Schlosspark, Bad Homburg vor der Hohe, 61348 Hessen, Germany
location.neighbourhood: Schlosspark, north end of the pond

trees.story:
Nobody has dated this oak, and it is probably the oldest thing in the park. It is 5.39 metres round and 25 metres tall, measured in the autumn of 2021 by the dendrologist who catalogued this park's big trees, and that girth puts it well past the cedars that have a planting date on them.

It stands just left of the bridge at the north end of the pond, on ground that has been garden since at least 1441, when a garden is first recorded beside the castle here. The park was laid out as a baroque garden from 1680 under Landgrave Friedrich II and remade as an English landscape park from the later eighteenth century, which is the style it still wears: grass, water, and single large trees given room. An oak this wide was either kept through one of those remakings or planted at one of them.

We would like to know which, and so would anyone standing under it. If you have a source for its age, a plaque, a park survey, a local record, tell us and we will put it on the page.

Single-sourced on measurements: the baumkunde.de forum thread on the Schlosspark records 5.39m girth and 25m height, measured by Rainer Lippert between 28 September and 2 October 2021, at 50 13 41.4 N / 8 36 29.9 E, left of the bridge at the northern end of the pond. NOT the Naturdenkmal 'Eiche am Forellenteich', which is a different oak of 4.30m in Dornholzhausen, 2.5 km away. No photograph found under an open licence.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by standing at the bridge over the north end of the pond and looking left: it is the broad oak immediately beside the bridge, a good deal thicker through the trunk than any other oak on that side of the water.

trees.name: The Oak South-West of the Lake

location.address: About 30 metres south-west of the lake, Schlosspark, Bad Homburg vor der Hohe, 61348 Hessen, Germany

trees.story:
This pedunculate oak is 4.94 metres round, measured in August 2021, and it stands about thirty metres south-west of the lake rather than on its bank, which is where our map first put it. A reader who knows this park tree by tree told us so, and the survey that measured it says the same.

It is one of three big oaks in the Schlosspark and the easiest to walk past. The largest, 5.39 metres, stands at the bridge two hundred metres north; a third, which locals call the Schöne Eiche, grows on the far side of the big meadow from the plane, towards the gate into the old town. This one has no name, no plaque and no path leading to it. It simply stands back from the water, broad and low-limbed, where the grass runs under the crown.

It is the common oak of German parkland, and at this girth almost certainly older than the cedars by the palace that carry a planting year. Nobody has dated it. The park was laid out as a baroque garden from 1680 and remade as an English landscape park a century later, and a trunk this wide was either kept through one of those remakings or planted at one of them. No source says which.

Our pin had been transcribed as 33.3" N, about 60m too far south; corrected to the source coordinate. The earlier ambiguity is resolved: his Schone Eiche (about 5m) is a THIRD oak, not this one and not bhg_003, near the gate to the Altstadt on the far side of the big meadow from the plane. Kept as a lead until he gives a spot, since a pin is the one field we cannot guess.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by standing at the lake in the southern half of the park: it is the broad oak on the water's edge, the only one of its size down there. The other large oak is at the bridge, two hundred metres north.
trees.recognise: Stands alone about thirty metres back from the south-west shore of the lake, not on the bank; the only big oak on that side of the water.

trees.name: The Plane by the Wingnuts

location.address: About ten metres east of the second wingnut, Schlosspark, Bad Homburg vor der Hohe, 61348 Hessen, Germany
location.neighbourhood: Schlosspark, north end of the pond

trees.story:
At 5.66 metres round, this is the thickest trunk anyone has measured in the park, wider than the famous cedars and wider than the big oak thirty metres away. It has no name, no plaque and no entry in any register. It turned up in a dendrologist's survey of the park in 2021 and that is the whole of its paper trail.

It stands about ten metres east of the second of the park's wingnuts, near the north end of the pond. Planes are easy to pick out once the eye knows them: bark that flakes off in irregular plates and leaves the trunk patched in olive, cream and grey, a pattern that keeps changing as the tree sheds, and seed balls that hang on bare branches through the winter like small brown lanterns.

We have not established which plane it is. The London plane is the usual one in a park of this date, but nobody has said so in print about this tree, so we have not written it down as fact. If you can tell an oriental plane from a London plane by the leaf lobes or the seed balls, stand under it and tell us.
